title: Installing ansible-core
shortDescription: Install and verify RHEL-provided and upstream ansible-core distributions.
description: Compare supported Python combinations, install the RHEL-provided ansible-core RPM, and install upstream ansible-core from PyPI in an isolated RHEL 9 environment.
coverAlt: RHEL terminal showing the installed ansible-core package and Ansible version
outcomes: Connect RHEL to Red Hat services
Install and inspect the RHEL-provided ansible-core RPM
Select a maintained upstream ansible-core and compatible Python release
Install upstream ansible-core from PyPI without replacing RHEL's system Python
Identify the collection namespace available from ansible-core
Validate a working Ansible control node

overview.title: What is ansible-core?
overview.introduction: ansible-core is the minimal automation engine at the center of Ansible automation. Developers and automation content authors use it to build, test, troubleshoot, and validate inventories, playbooks, roles, plugins, and collections before moving approved content into an operational workflow.

items.title: Built-in command-line tools
items.detail: The package installs commands for running playbooks, inspecting inventory and configuration, reading documentation, installing collections, encrypting sensitive data, and testing automation content. These include ansible, ansible-playbook, ansible-inventory, ansible-config, ansible-doc, ansible-galaxy, ansible-vault, and ansible-test.

items.title: Automation language
items.detail: ansible-core processes playbooks written in YAML. Playbooks can contain tasks, handlers, variables, conditions, loops, imports, and includes.

items.title: Execution runtime
items.detail: It reads inventory, connects to managed nodes, loads the required plugins, and runs modules. The same engine can be invoked from a developer's terminal or through a controller.

items.title: Built-in content
items.detail: It includes the modules and plugins in the ansible.builtin namespace. This content ships with ansible-core and does not require a separate collection installation.

items.title: Additional collections
items.detail: Install collections separately when your automation needs modules, plugins, roles, or other content that is not included in ansible.builtin.

overview.note: In the following demonstrations, you will use the local ansible-core CLI to develop and validate automation. Teams that need shared credentials, controlled access, approvals, scheduling, and audit history should run approved production jobs through a controller or orchestration platform. The platform manages the workflow; an Ansible runtime executes the automation.

orchestrationOptions.title: Common platforms for shared Ansible operations
orchestrationOptions.introduction: These platforms provide a shared interface for running automation, controlling access, and reviewing job results. Their scope, Ansible integration, and support models differ.

items.title: Automation Controller
items.detail: The Red Hat-supported enterprise controller included with Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform. It provides centralized credentials, access controls, job templates, workflows, schedules, APIs, job history, and auditing.

items.title: AWX
items.detail: The upstream community project from which Automation Controller is developed. It provides a web interface, REST API, and task engine for Ansible. AWX is self-supported, so review its release, deployment, and upgrade model before using it in production.

items.title: Semaphore UI
items.detail: A self-hosted web interface and API for running Ansible and other automation tools. It provides projects, repositories, inventories, protected credentials, task templates, schedules, logs, and role-based access. Community and commercial editions are available.

items.title: Rundeck
items.detail: A runbook automation platform that can include Ansible in larger operational workflows. Its Ansible integration can import inventory and run modules or playbooks. Rundeck manages the workflow while Ansible performs the Ansible-specific execution.

orchestrationOptions.note: Check how each platform handles execution isolation, secrets, permissions, approvals, audit records, availability, scaling, upgrades, integrations, and support. Links to dedicated HODs can be added as those demonstrations are published.

relatedTools.title: ansible-navigator
relatedTools.detail: ansible-navigator is installed separately from ansible-core. Red Hat documentation refers to it as automation content navigator. It gives developers command-line and interactive interfaces for running, inspecting, and troubleshooting Ansible content, often through execution environments. These environments normally contain ansible-core, the required collections, and their dependencies. A future HOD will cover its installation, downloading an execution environment, and running a test command.

prerequisites.label: System
prerequisites.detail: A current RHEL 9 physical or virtual machine.

prerequisites.label: Access
prerequisites.detail: A user that can run administrative commands with sudo.

prerequisites.label: Connectivity
prerequisites.detail: Outbound access to Red Hat registration and content services.

accessCallout.title: Don’t have a Red Hat subscription?
accessCallout.detail: You can join the Red Hat Developer program at no cost. Eligible members can activate the self-supported Red Hat Developer Subscription for Individuals, which provides access to RHEL and repositories such as BaseOS and AppStream. You do not need an Ansible Automation Platform subscription to complete this lab. The Developer Subscription gives you access to the packages used here, but it does not include product support for automation you create with ansible-core.

comparisons.title: RHEL-provided ansible-core vs upstream ansible-core
comparisons.introduction: RHEL provides ansible-core as an AppStream RPM, while the upstream Ansible project publishes it as a Python distribution on PyPI. These distributions differ in package management, Python integration, release cadence, maintenance lifecycle, and support.

notes.title: What stays the same
notes.detail: Both distributions provide the ansible-core command-line tools, automation language, execution runtime, and embedded ansible.builtin collection. Other collections are installed and maintained separately.

notes.title: Package access
notes.detail: A RHEL subscription provides access to the AppStream RPM. Package access and support for automation created with ansible-core are separate; see Support coverage in the comparison below.

values: A Red Hat-built and signed RPM installed with DNF from the RHEL AppStream repository. DNF manages its files, dependencies, signatures, updates, and errata.
A Python distribution published by the upstream project. Install it with pip in a virtual environment or use pipx to create an isolated application environment.
DNF selects the RHEL filesystem locations and platform Python dependencies. The commands are available system-wide and remain under RPM control.

You select the Python interpreter and installation environment. You are responsible for its dependencies, upgrades, and removal. Do not use pip to overwrite the RPM-managed installation or add packages to RHEL's platform Python; use a virtual environment or pipx.
RHEL 9 provides the ansible-core 2.14 Full Life Application Stream. Red Hat can update the RPM release while retaining the 2.14 feature baseline.

Upstream normally publishes a new X.Y feature release about every six months and X.Y.Z patch releases about every four weeks. New features and support for newer Python versions become available here first.

Maintenance follows the RHEL and AppStream lifecycle. Red Hat can backport fixes without changing the upstream feature version, so assess the package through Red Hat advisories and security data rather than its version number alone.

The upstream project maintains three X.Y releases at graduated levels. The newest receives general bug and security fixes, the next receives critical and security fixes, and the oldest receives security fixes. Unmaintained releases generally receive no further fixes.
Use the Python dependencies selected by DNF for the RPM. Do not apply the upstream PyPI control-node matrix to this installation.

Select a maintained ansible-core release that supports the Python version in your chosen environment. Test playbooks before changing X.Y releases because ansible-core does not guarantee complete compatibility between feature releases.

Red Hat supports this RPM when it is used with playbooks, roles, and modules included with or generated by Red Hat products. Examples include RHEL System Roles, remediation playbooks generated by Red Hat Insights, and task playbooks generated by Red Hat Insights. Support for the underlying Ansible platform and core-maintained modules outside this scope requires an Ansible Automation Platform subscription.

Maintained releases receive updates, documentation, issue tracking, and community collaboration from the upstream project. Installing ansible-core from PyPI does not create a Red Hat product-support entitlement.

reference.label: Read Red Hat's ansible-core support scope

comparisons.takeaway: Use the AppStream RPM when RHEL integration and DNF-managed maintenance are the priority. Use the upstream PyPI distribution when you need a newer maintained ansible-core release or Python combination. For an upstream installation, keep ansible-core in a virtual environment or a pipx-managed environment so that pip-owned packages remain separate from the operating system's managed Python environment.

comparisons.title: RHEL-provided ansible-core compatibility
comparisons.introduction: RHEL packages ansible-core with a control-node Python runtime selected for each RHEL major release. Managed-host requirements depend on the operating system, connection method, module, and collection. The table covers the ansible-core baseline for Linux, Unix, and Windows hosts; individual collections and modules can set narrower requirements. It lists feature streams rather than exact RPM builds, so the installed 2.14.z or 2.16.z version can change through updates. Red Hat maintains these RPMs under the RHEL lifecycle, independently of the upstream lifecycle.

notes.title: Linux and Unix hosts
notes.detail: Ansible is not installed on the managed host. Most modules need one supported Python interpreter from the range or alternatives listed below; the host does not need every Python version shown. It also needs an account that Ansible can reach over SSH. When a task must run as root, that account needs permission to use sudo or another configured become method. The ansible.builtin.raw module can help bootstrap a host that does not yet have Python.

notes.title: Windows hosts
notes.detail: Windows modules run through Windows PowerShell rather than Python. The host also needs a supported Windows release and a configured connection. The versioned ansible-core guidance shown here uses WinRM; individual modules can require a newer Windows, PowerShell, or .NET Framework version.

notes.title: Network devices and appliances
notes.detail: Network modules commonly use collection-specific connection plugins and do not require Python on the managed device. Check the collection, module, connection-plugin, operating-system, and device-vendor documentation for additional transport, library, firmware, or platform requirements.

comparisons.title: Upstream ansible-core compatibility
comparisons.introduction: The upstream Ansible project publishes ansible-core as a Python distribution on PyPI. Compatibility must be checked at both ends of the connection: the Python interpreter that runs ansible-core on the control node and the runtime used to execute modules on each managed host. Linux and Unix hosts normally use Python, Windows hosts use PowerShell and .NET, and network devices often follow collection- and connection-plugin-specific requirements instead. The matrix covers ansible-base 2.10 through the latest published release and includes lifecycle dates because a compatible release is not necessarily a maintained release.

demos.title: Install and validate ansible-core on RHEL 9
demos.objective: Register a RHEL 9 system, install the AppStream ansible-core RPM, inspect its content boundary, and prove that the runtime can execute a module locally.
outcomes: Connect RHEL to Red Hat services and verify BaseOS and AppStream
Install and inspect the Red Hat-provided ansible-core RPM
Validate the control node with a localhost module test

steps.label: Verify
steps.title: Verify the RHEL 9 starting environment
steps.alt: Clean Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 desktop with a terminal ready for commands
steps.explanation: Confirm the operating system, processor architecture, hostname, and clean package state before making changes. This recording uses RHEL 9 on aarch64; your architecture and hostname may differ.
steps.expected: The host reports RHEL 9, a supported architecture, its own hostname, and that ansible-core is not installed.
steps.note: The demonstration VM was fully upgraded before recording. On an existing system, rpm may report an installed package; compare its version before continuing.
steps.troubleshooting: If the system is not RHEL 9, stop and use installation guidance for that operating system. If ansible-core is already installed, this lab can still be used to inspect and verify it.

steps.label: Register
steps.title: Connect the system to Red Hat
steps.alt: RHEL terminal confirming successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Insights
steps.explanation: The rhc client prompts interactively for your Red Hat account and connects the host to Subscription Management and Insights. Enter credentials only at those prompts—never place them in a command, recording, transcript, or script.
steps.expected: rhc reports successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Insights and activates remote host configuration.
steps.note: Credential input is excluded from the replay. The neutral placeholders show where learners interact without exposing an account name or password.
steps.troubleshooting: If no credential prompt appears, make sure rhc connect is running in an interactive terminal. If registration fails, verify network, DNS, proxy, system time, and the account's RHEL entitlement.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.title: Confirm the Red Hat connections
steps.alt: RHEL terminal showing active Subscription Management and Red Hat Insights connections
steps.explanation: Verify the result independently after rhc connect finishes. The two service connection lines confirm that the host can obtain subscribed content and report to Insights.
steps.expected: The system is connected to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Insights.
steps.note: The remote host configuration daemon may later report inactive. That optional daemon state does not prevent DNF from installing ansible-core from subscribed repositories.
steps.troubleshooting: If either required connection is unavailable, retry rhc connect and review network, DNS, proxy, time synchronization, and entitlement access before continuing.

steps.label: Repositories
steps.title: Verify the enabled repositories
steps.alt: DNF output listing enabled RHEL BaseOS and AppStream repositories
steps.command:
sudo subscription-manager repos --list-enabled
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
steps.explanation: subscription-manager shows the repositories enabled in the Red Hat subscription configuration. dnf repolist shows the enabled repositories DNF can currently use. BaseOS supplies the operating-system foundation; AppStream contains ansible-core and several dependencies.
steps.expected: Both the RHEL 9 BaseOS and AppStream RPM repositories appear as enabled.
steps.note: Repository IDs include the architecture. This recording uses aarch64; x86_64 systems show corresponding x86_64 repository IDs.
steps.troubleshooting: If either repository is missing, refresh subscription data, then enable the architecture-specific BaseOS and AppStream repository IDs shown in the troubleshooting guide.

steps.label: Inspect
steps.title: Inspect the RHEL-provided package
steps.alt: DNF repoquery output showing ansible-core package information
steps.explanation: Inspecting the package before installation confirms its version, architecture, source repository, size, license, and purpose. The exact version will change as Red Hat publishes updates.
steps.expected: The latest ansible-core build is available from the RHEL 9 AppStream repository.
steps.troubleshooting: If DNF reports no matching package, verify that AppStream is enabled, clean the DNF metadata, and rebuild the cache.

steps.label: Install
steps.title: Install ansible-core with DNF
steps.alt: DNF transaction completing the ansible-core installation
steps.explanation: DNF resolves and installs ansible-core plus required Python, SSH, and Git dependencies. Review the transaction summary before confirming the installation in your environment.
steps.expected: The transaction finishes with Complete! and lists ansible-core among the installed packages.
steps.troubleshooting: If dependency resolution fails, refresh package metadata and review the transaction without disabling signature checks or forcing package removal.

steps.label: Validate
steps.title: Confirm the package and runtime
steps.alt: Terminal output showing the ansible-core RPM and Ansible version details
steps.command:
rpm -q ansible-core
rpm -V ansible-core && echo "Package verification: passed"
dnf list --installed ansible-core
command -v ansible
command -v ansible-playbook
ansible --version
steps.explanation: Confirm the installed RPM, verify that its packaged files are unchanged, locate both primary command-line tools, and inspect the runtime. The version output identifies the active configuration file, Python runtime, module paths, and collection paths.
steps.expected: All commands return successfully and ansible --version reports the installed core release.
steps.troubleshooting: If rpm -V prints file differences, investigate them before relying on the installation. If the shell cannot find ansible, start a new terminal or run hash -r, then check /usr/bin/ansible.

steps.label: Collections
steps.title: Inspect the available collection namespace
steps.alt: Terminal showing ansible.builtin as the single collection namespace exposed by module documentation
steps.command:
ansible-doc --list | cut -d. -f1,2 | grep '^ansible\.' | sort -u
ansible-doc --list | cut -d. -f1,2 | grep '^ansible\.' | sort -u | wc -l
steps.explanation: ansible-doc --list prints documented modules by fully qualified collection name. cut keeps the namespace and collection portions, grep retains Ansible collection names, and sort -u removes duplicates. The first command therefore shows which collection namespaces supply the available modules; the second adds wc -l to count those unique names.
steps.expected: On this clean RHEL ansible-core installation, the commands show ansible.builtin and then the count 1. This makes the minimal content boundary visible before later labs install other collections.
steps.note: This is a count of collection namespaces represented in the module documentation index—not a count of modules or plugins. ansible.builtin is embedded in ansible-core, so ansible-galaxy collection list, which inventories separately installed collection artifacts in collection paths, may not list it and can report that no usable collection path exists on a clean system.
steps.troubleshooting: If additional names appear, the system can already discover modules from other collections. Check ansible --version for collection paths and inspect those paths before comparing your result with this clean VM; do not remove existing collections blindly.

steps.label: Explore
steps.title: Inspect configuration and module help
steps.alt: Terminal showing Ansible configuration and ping module documentation
steps.command:
PAGER=cat ansible-config dump --only-changed
PAGER=cat ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.ping
steps.explanation: PAGER=cat sets the pager only for the command that follows, so output is written directly to the terminal instead of opening an interactive viewer such as less. ansible-config dump prints Ansible's resolved configuration, and --only-changed limits the result to values that differ from built-in defaults. The second command confirms that built-in module documentation is available; ansible.builtin.ping is the module's fully qualified collection name.
steps.expected: Ansible shows the active configuration file or other settings that differ from defaults, then displays the argument summary for ansible.builtin.ping. On a system with no changed settings, the first command can legitimately produce little or no output.
steps.note: PAGER=cat is a temporary environment-variable assignment for one command; it does not permanently change your shell or Ansible configuration. Omit it when you prefer paged output in a normal terminal.
steps.troubleshooting: If ansible-doc cannot find the module, confirm ansible-core is installed and that the Ansible executable and Python environment come from the expected RHEL package.

steps.label: Test
steps.title: Run a functional smoke test
steps.alt: Ansible localhost ping module returning a successful pong response
steps.explanation: This is an Ansible ad hoc command: ansible starts the CLI, localhost is the target host pattern, -m selects a module, and ansible.builtin.ping is the fully qualified module name. The -c local option uses Ansible's local connection instead of SSH, so the module runs on this control node without an inventory or remote host. Unlike the operating-system ping utility, this module does not send ICMP packets; it verifies that Ansible can execute Python and return JSON successfully.
steps.expected: localhost returns SUCCESS with ping: pong and changed: false.
steps.note: You now have a working Ansible control node and can continue with inventories, playbooks, and collections.
steps.troubleshooting: An implicit-inventory warning can be normal for this localhost-only test. The important result is localhost | SUCCESS and ping: pong.

troubleshooting.title: rhc connect cannot register the system
troubleshooting.detail: Confirm internet access, DNS resolution, an accurate system clock, and any required proxy configuration. Verify that the Red Hat account has an active RHEL entitlement, then retry rhc connect.

troubleshooting.title: BaseOS or AppStream is not enabled
troubleshooting.command:
sudo subscription-manager refresh
sudo subscription-manager repos \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-baseos-rpms" \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-appstream-rpms"
troubleshooting.detail: Refresh the entitlement data and enable the repository IDs that match the system architecture. Run dnf repolist --enabled again to confirm both repositories.

troubleshooting.title: DNF reports: No match for argument ansible-core
troubleshooting.command:
sudo dnf clean all
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf repoquery --latest-limit 1 ansible-core
troubleshooting.detail: This usually means AppStream is unavailable or the local metadata is stale. Rebuild the cache only after confirming the repository is enabled.

troubleshooting.title: The localhost smoke test shows a warning
troubleshooting.detail: A warning about the implicit localhost or an empty inventory is expected in this inventory-free test. Continue if the result contains SUCCESS and ping: pong.

troubleshooting.title: The collection inventory shows more than ansible.builtin
troubleshooting.detail: Additional collection namespaces mean this environment is not limited to the clean ansible-core content shown in the demonstration. Use the collection paths from ansible --version to locate separately installed content. A missing collection directory on a clean system is not an ansible-core installation failure.

verification: rhc status reports active Subscription Management and Insights connections
rpm -q ansible-core returns the installed package
rpm -V ansible-core reports no package-file differences
The module documentation inventory shows the ansible.builtin collection namespace
ansible-config and ansible-doc return usable output
The localhost ping test returns SUCCESS and ping: pong

cleanup.explanation: Cleanup is optional. Remove the package only if this VM will not be used for later Ansible labs. Unregistering also removes access to subscribed RHEL content.
cleanup.command:
sudo dnf remove ansible-core
# Optional: disconnect this disposable lab VM
sudo rhc disconnect

demos.title: Install upstream ansible-core from PyPI on RHEL 9
demos.objective: Install a supported Python from subscribed RHEL repositories, isolate it in a virtual environment, install upstream ansible-core from PyPI, and verify both its content boundary and runtime behavior.
outcomes: Select a maintained upstream ansible-core and compatible control-node Python
Install RHEL Python 3.12 without replacing the platform Python
Create an isolated virtual environment for Ansible
Install upstream ansible-core from PyPI rather than a RHEL RPM
Verify package provenance, content boundary, activation, and runtime behavior

steps.label: Assess
steps.title: Assess the clean RHEL Python environment
steps.alt: RHEL terminal showing Python 3.9, no Python 3.12, no pip, and no ansible-core RPM
steps.command:
cat /etc/redhat-release
uname -m
rpm -q ansible-core
python3 --version
command -v python3.12 || echo "Python 3.12 is not installed"
python3 -m pip --version
steps.explanation: Establish the operating system, architecture, package state, default interpreter, and pip availability before selecting an upstream release. On RHEL 9, the unversioned python3 command remains the platform Python 3.9. Current maintained upstream ansible-core releases require a newer control-node Python, so do not let pip silently resolve an obsolete ansible-core release merely to fit Python 3.9.
steps.expected: The host reports RHEL 9 and its architecture, the ansible-core RPM is absent, Python 3.9 is the default, and Python 3.12 and pip are not yet available on this reset VM.
steps.note: Consult the upstream compatibility matrix above before choosing a Python and ansible-core pair. This recording uses ansible-core 2.21 with Python 3.12.
steps.troubleshooting: If ansible-core or Python 3.12 is already present, identify who installed it and where it lives before continuing. Do not remove an existing runtime from a shared system merely to reproduce the clean-state messages.

steps.label: Select Python
steps.title: Verify the repositories and Python 3.12 packages
steps.alt: DNF listing subscribed RHEL repositories and available Python 3.12 packages
steps.command:
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf list --available python3.12 python3.12-pip
steps.explanation: Confirm that BaseOS and AppStream are enabled, then inspect the versioned interpreter and matching pip package before installation. The RHEL subscription is used here to obtain supported Python packages from AppStream; it is not used to obtain ansible-core in this demonstration.
steps.expected: DNF lists enabled BaseOS and AppStream repositories and shows python3.12 plus python3.12-pip as available AppStream packages.
steps.note: Repository IDs and package architecture vary between aarch64 and x86_64 systems. Match the package names and behavior rather than the recorded architecture or exact patch version.
steps.troubleshooting: If the packages are unavailable, confirm registration, refresh subscription data, enable BaseOS and AppStream for the system architecture, and rebuild DNF metadata. Python 3.12 first appeared in RHEL 9.4, so an older pinned RHEL 9 content set must be updated or adjusted.

steps.label: Install Python
steps.title: Install the compatible Python prerequisite
steps.alt: DNF completing the Python 3.12 and pip installation on RHEL 9
steps.explanation: Install the versioned Python 3.12 interpreter and its matching pip package with DNF. The -y option accepts the displayed transaction non-interactively; omit it when you want to approve the transaction manually. This does not replace RHEL's platform Python 3.9 and does not install an ansible-core RPM.
steps.expected: DNF installs Python 3.12, pip and their dependencies, then returns Complete! and a fresh shell prompt.
steps.troubleshooting: If dependency resolution or signature verification fails, refresh repository metadata and investigate the repository or entitlement problem. Do not disable signature checks, replace the system Python, or force-remove platform packages.

steps.label: Isolate
steps.title: Create and activate a Python 3.12 virtual environment
steps.alt: Terminal creating and activating an ansible-core Python 3.12 virtual environment
steps.command:
python3.12 --version
python3.12 -m pip --version
mkdir -p ~/.venvs
python3.12 -m venv --prompt ansible-core-2.21 ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21
source ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21/bin/activate
python --version
python -m pip --version
steps.explanation: Verify the selected interpreter, create a user-owned virtual environment, and activate it. python3.12 -m venv guarantees which interpreter builds the environment; --prompt supplies a recognizable shell label. After activation, the unversioned python and pip commands resolve inside the environment rather than modifying RHEL's system package locations.
steps.expected: Python reports version 3.12, the prompt identifies ansible-core-2.21, and pip's location is under /home/rajat/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21.
steps.note: Red Hat recommends a virtual environment or a non-root --user installation for third-party Python packages. This demonstration uses a virtual environment for isolation, repeatability and easy cleanup.
steps.troubleshooting: If venv creation fails, confirm that python3.12 and python3.12-pip are installed. If activation succeeds but python still points to /usr/bin, inspect PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV, then open a clean Bash shell and activate the environment again.

steps.label: Install Core
steps.title: Install upstream ansible-core from PyPI
steps.alt: pip downloading and installing upstream ansible-core 2.21.2 and its dependencies from PyPI
steps.command:
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install ansible-core==2.21.2
steps.explanation: Upgrade pip inside the active virtual environment, then install a specific upstream ansible-core release for reproducibility. python -m pip binds the package operation to the active environment's interpreter. The download URLs and wheel names in the replay show the upstream Python distribution being obtained through PyPI rather than a RHEL RPM repository.
steps.expected: pip successfully installs ansible-core 2.21.2 and its Python dependencies inside the virtual environment.
steps.note: Pinning 2.21.2 makes this verified replay repeatable. When creating your own environment, consult the current support matrix and intentionally select a maintained version instead of copying an old pin indefinitely.
steps.troubleshooting: If pip reports that no matching distribution exists, compare the active Python version with the upstream support matrix. Also verify DNS, HTTPS access to PyPI, proxy settings and the system clock; do not add --break-system-packages because this installation belongs in the virtual environment.

steps.label: Prove Source
steps.title: Verify the package owner, paths and runtime
steps.alt: Terminal proving ansible-core is pip-managed inside a Python 3.12 virtual environment
steps.command:
rpm -q ansible-core
command -v python
command -v ansible
python -m pip show ansible-core
python -m pip check
ansible --version
steps.explanation: Use independent checks to establish what was installed and who owns it. The RPM query remains negative, the executables and package location point into ~/.venvs, pip identifies ansible-core 2.21.2 and validates its dependencies, and ansible --version confirms the active executable, Python runtime, module path and collection paths.
steps.expected: No ansible-core RPM is installed; pip reports ansible-core 2.21.2 with no broken requirements; Python and Ansible paths both belong to the virtual environment.
steps.troubleshooting: If command -v resolves /usr/bin/ansible or another environment, deactivate competing environments, inspect PATH, and activate ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21 again before repeating every verification command.

steps.label: Collections
steps.title: Inspect the upstream content boundary
steps.alt: Terminal showing no separately installed collections and the embedded ansible namespace
steps.command:
ansible-galaxy collection list
ansible-doc -l 2>/dev/null | awk -F. '{print $1}' | sort -u
PAGER=cat ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.ping
steps.explanation: Separate installed collection artifacts and embedded core content are different inventories. ansible-galaxy collection list checks configured collection paths and can warn that none exist on this clean environment. ansible-doc indexes usable module documentation; extracting its first namespace shows ansible, and the final command proves that the embedded ansible.builtin.ping documentation is available.
steps.expected: No separately installed collection path is usable, the documented module namespace is ansible, and ansible.builtin.ping help is displayed.
steps.note: The stderr redirection on the namespace command keeps a known internal-development warning out of this concise derived list; it does not change the ansible-doc result. The upstream ansible-core distribution does not include the separate ansible community package or its curated collection set.
steps.troubleshooting: If additional namespaces or collection paths appear, this is not a clean minimal environment. Use ansible --version and ansible-galaxy collection list to identify the discovered paths before deciding whether the extra content is intentional.

steps.label: Test
steps.title: Run a functional localhost smoke test
steps.alt: Upstream ansible-core returning pong from a successful localhost module test
steps.explanation: Run the same functional test used for the RHEL RPM so the two distributions are compared by behavior, not only by version output. localhost selects the implicit local host, -m chooses ansible.builtin.ping, and -c local executes through the local connection instead of SSH. The module validates Python execution and JSON return data; it does not send an ICMP packet.
steps.expected: localhost returns SUCCESS with changed: false and ping: pong.
steps.troubleshooting: The implicit-inventory warning is expected because this focused test does not supply an inventory. Investigate only if the result does not contain localhost | SUCCESS and ping: pong.

steps.label: Use It
steps.title: Understand activation and shell scope
steps.alt: Terminal activating and deactivating the ansible-core virtual environment
steps.command:
command -v ansible || echo "ansible is not on PATH outside the virtual environment"
source ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21/bin/activate
ansible --version | head -1
deactivate
command -v ansible || echo "ansible is not on PATH outside the virtual environment"
steps.explanation: A virtual environment is isolated by design. Its Ansible commands become available when activation prepends the environment's bin directory to PATH, and disappear from PATH after deactivate. Activate the environment in each new shell before running Ansible, or invoke an executable through its full ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21/bin path.
steps.expected: Ansible is absent from PATH before activation, reports core 2.21.2 while active, and is absent again after deactivation.
steps.note: Activation changes only the current shell. It does not start a service, install a daemon, or modify other users' sessions.
steps.troubleshooting: If ansible remains available after deactivate, another installation also exists on PATH. Run type -a ansible and inspect every returned location before choosing which installation to use.

troubleshooting.title: Python 3.12 packages are unavailable
troubleshooting.command:
sudo subscription-manager refresh
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf clean metadata
sudo dnf makecache
troubleshooting.detail: Confirm a registered RHEL system, enabled BaseOS and AppStream repositories, an eligible RHEL 9 content set, working DNS and current metadata before retrying the package query.

troubleshooting.title: pip cannot resolve the requested ansible-core
troubleshooting.command:
python --version
python -m pip --version
python -m pip index versions ansible-core
troubleshooting.detail: Verify that the virtual environment uses a Python version supported by the requested ansible-core release and that the host can reach PyPI through any required proxy.

troubleshooting.title: The wrong Ansible executable runs
troubleshooting.command:
type -a ansible
echo "$VIRTUAL_ENV"
source ~/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21/bin/activate
command -v ansible
troubleshooting.detail: Inspect every executable on PATH, activate the intended environment, and confirm its bin directory wins before testing the runtime.

troubleshooting.title: The localhost test reports an inventory warning
troubleshooting.detail: The implicit-localhost warning is expected without an inventory. The functional acceptance criterion is localhost SUCCESS with ping pong.

verification: Python 3.12 and its matching pip package were installed from subscribed RHEL AppStream repositories
The virtual environment uses Python 3.12 and stores packages under /home/rajat/.venvs/ansible-core-2.21
rpm reports that the RHEL ansible-core package is not installed
pip reports upstream ansible-core 2.21.2 and no broken requirements
The embedded ansible.builtin namespace is usable without separately installed collections
The localhost ping test returns SUCCESS and ping: pong
Activation and deactivation correctly add and remove the environment's Ansible executable from PATH

cleanup.explanation: Cleanup removes only the user-owned upstream ansible-core environment created by this demonstration. Python 3.12 remains installed because other applications may use it; remove operating-system packages only after checking dependencies and local policy.
